newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Singapore Internet gets boost from television link.
newsitem.headline: Singapore Internet gets boost from television link.

text.p: Singapore's Internet users will be able to access multimedia services using broadcast links to cable television, officials of MediaManager, the operator of the service, said on Thursday.
This first interactive broadcast service allows users to receive multimedia sound and images at higher speeds via television antennas rather than traditional dial-up phone lines.
"It looks more like a combination of TV and Internet because we have much higher speeds," said Adrian Rietberg, managing director of MediaManager.
He told reporters the advantages of interactive broadcast were its high speeds of up to 20 megabit per second (mbps) for TV, 40 mbps for satellite -- 1,000 times faster than phone lines.
Rietberg said another advantage was that the phone line used for the Internet could be freed up. The connection through the TV would also not disrupt viewing of programmes, he said.
The Singapore Broadcast Authority (SBA) awarded MediaManager the broadcast licence but could permit others to provide similar service although capacity is currently limited.
The Data Cast service packages a selection of sites commonly visited by users such as Internet newspapers, web pages such as movie-guides and music hit charts.
"The survey helps us to identify which are the web sites Singaporeans like to see. Those are the web sites we've captured, will broadcast and publish here," Rietberg said.
He said about 33 web sites generated about 50 percent of all Internet traffic.
The daily local newspaper The Straits Times, CNN, BBC, Microsoft, Netscape, Yahoo, Discovery channel, National Geographic, games and business software were favourite sites.
Data Cast will rely on Singapore Telecommunications' SingNet Internet gateway to provide data feed for its broadcast.
MediaManager also launched on Thursday its access to the Internet called Smart.Net, offering such services as email accounts.
Rietberg said users must now buy a decoder receiver card or box to obtain the service, but these will become standard items in computers next year.
The company hopes to sign on some 25,000 users by the end of 1998.
